item.title: The inflammatory reflex as a stochastic dynamical system
item.dc:creator: Matías Castillo-Aguilar
item.description:
Original Article · Vol. I · No. 11 · November 2026

1 The circuit

The nervous system does not merely find out about inflammation: it regulates it. Cytokines released in the periphery activate afferent fibres of the vagus nerve; the brainstem responds through the efferent branch, and that cholinergic signal ends up restraining the release of tumour necrosis factor by macrophages. It is a reflex arc in the strict sense, known as the inflammatory reflex [1].

The classic experimental evidence has two sides. In rats exposed to endotoxin, cutting the vagus increases the cytokine response, and stimulating it electrically attenuates it [2]. A good minimal model should reproduce both.

2 The model

We use three dimensionless variables: the load of the inflammatory stimulus , the concentration of a pro-inflammatory cytokine and the efferent vagal activity .

The stimulus is cleared at rate . The cytokine is produced in proportion to the stimulus, but vagal activity divides that production (the cholinergic brake), and it is eliminated at rate . The third equation is the reflex: is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process whose mean is no longer constant but rises with the cytokine in a saturable way, with gain . The noise in is multiplicative, so the concentration never becomes negative; the noise in is additive.

A teaching model

The parameters in Table I are illustrative: they were chosen so that the cytokine peaks between one and two hours after the stimulus, as happens qualitatively with endotoxin, but they are not fitted to data. For models of acute inflammation with a detailed analysis, see [3].

3 Implementation

The system is non-linear, so there is no exact transition and we fall back on Euler–Maruyama, with a step fifty times smaller than the fastest time constant. The function simulates n paths at once and allows two interventions: severing the efferent branch and stimulating the nerve during a time window.

par <- list(k_P = 0.5, k_C = 2, d_C = 0.9, K_V = 1, V0 = 1, g = 3,
            K_C = 0.5, tau_V = 0.25, sigma_C = 0.35, sigma_V = 0.6)

simulate <- function(par, n = 1, hours = 12, dt = 0.005, P0 = 1,
                     efferent = TRUE, stimulus = 0, window = c(0, 2)) {
  steps <- round(hours / dt)
  t <- seq(0, hours, by = dt)
  P <- P0 * exp(-par$k_P * t)                      # exact solution of dP
  C <- V <- matrix(0, steps + 1, n)
  V[1, ] <- par$V0
  for (i in seq_len(steps)) {
    u <- if (t[i] >= window[1] && t[i] < window[2]) stimulus else 0
    brake <- if (efferent) 1 / (1 + pmax(V[i, ], 0) / par$K_V) else 1
    dW <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n, 0, sqrt(dt)), nrow = 2)
    C[i + 1, ] <- C[i, ] +
      (par$k_C * P[i] * brake - par$d_C * C[i, ]) * dt +
      par$sigma_C * C[i, ] * dW[1, ]
    target <- par$V0 + par$g * C[i, ] / (par$K_C + C[i, ]) + u
    V[i + 1, ] <- V[i, ] + (target - V[i, ]) / par$tau_V * dt +
      par$sigma_V * dW[2, ]
  }
  list(t = t, P = P, C = C, V = if (efferent) V else 0 * V)
}

4 Three experiments without noise

We first switch the noise off to see the deterministic skeleton, and repeat the classic experiments: intact reflex, vagotomy, and vagal stimulation during the first two hours.

no_noise <- modifyList(par, list(sigma_C = 0, sigma_V = 0))

conditions <- list(
  "Intact reflex"     = simulate(no_noise),
  "Vagotomy"          = simulate(no_noise, efferent = FALSE),
  "Vagal stimulation" = simulate(no_noise, stimulus = 3)
)

long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(conditions), function(name) {
  s <- conditions[[name]]
  i <- seq(1, length(s$t), by = 8)               # one point in eight is plenty
  rbind(
    data.frame(t = s$t[i], value = s$C[i, 1], condition = name,
               variable = "Cytokine C"),
    data.frame(t = s$t[i], value = s$V[i, 1], condition = name,
               variable = "Efferent vagal activity V")
  )
}))
long$condition <- factor(long$condition, levels = names(conditions))
long$variable <- factor(long$variable,
                        levels = c("Cytokine C", "Efferent vagal activity V"))

ggplot(long, aes(t, value, linetype = condition)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 12, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Time since stimulus (h)", y = NULL)
summary_tab <- t(sapply(conditions, function(s) {
  c(max(s$C), s$t[which.max(s$C)], sum(s$C) * 0.005)
}))
knitr::kable(summary_tab, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Peak", "Time of peak (h)", "AUC"))

The model reproduces both sides of the experiment. Without the efferent branch, the cytokine peak is 2.8 times the one reached with the reflex intact, and it arrives later; with stimulation, it falls to 58%. Note the bottom panel too: with the reflex intact, vagal activity rises on its own in response to the cytokine and returns to its basal tone once the inflammation resolves.

5 How much does the gain matter?

The gain summarises the sensitivity of the reflex arc. Sweeping it shows diminishing returns: most of the protection is obtained with moderate gains, because both the afferent pathway and the cholinergic brake saturate.

sweep_g <- data.frame(g = seq(0, 10, by = 0.25))
sweep_g$peak <- sapply(sweep_g$g, function(g) {
  max(simulate(modifyList(no_noise, list(g = g)))$C)
})

ggplot(sweep_g, aes(g, peak)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = subset(sweep_g, g == 3), size = 2.4) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = "Reflex gain, g", y = "Peak cytokine")

6 With noise: a distribution of responses

With the noise switched on, the same stimulus no longer produces one curve but a family of them. We simulate 2000 individuals with identical parameters.

set.seed(2002)
ensemble <- simulate(par, n = 2000)

idx <- seq(1, length(ensemble$t), by = 10)
q <- t(apply(ensemble$C[idx, ], 1, quantile,
             c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95)))
fan <- data.frame(t = ensemble$t[idx], q)
names(fan) <- c("t", "q05", "q25", "q50", "q75", "q95")

examples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(k) {
  data.frame(t = ensemble$t[idx], C = ensemble$C[idx, k], k = k)
}))

ggplot(fan, aes(t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), fill = "grey30", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = C, group = k), examples,
            linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 12, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Time since stimulus (h)", y = "Cytokine C")

The interesting question is what feedback does to that spread. We compare the distribution of the cytokine peak with the reflex active () and with a fixed vagal tone that does not respond to inflammation ().

set.seed(2002)
peaks_for <- function(g) {
  apply(simulate(modifyList(par, list(g = g)), n = 2000)$C, 2, max)
}
lv <- c("Fixed tone (g = 0)", "Active reflex (g = 3)")
peaks <- rbind(
  data.frame(condition = lv[1], peak = peaks_for(0)),
  data.frame(condition = lv[2], peak = peaks_for(3))
)
peaks$condition <- factor(peaks$condition, levels = lv)

ggplot(peaks, aes(peak, linetype = condition)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.55, key_glyph = "path") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid")) +
  labs(x = "Peak cytokine", y = "Density")
tab <- t(sapply(split(peaks$peak, peaks$condition), function(x) {
  c(mean(x), sd(x), sd(x) / mean(x), quantile(x, 0.95))
}))
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3, col.names = c("Mean", "SD", "CV", "P95"))

The reflex shifts the whole distribution to the left: the mean falls by 30% and the 95th percentile, which is where the dangerous responses live, by 33%. The absolute spread shrinks as well, although the coefficient of variation changes little: feedback mostly trims the scale of the response.

One detail is worth not missing: the mean peak with noise (0.49) is higher than the deterministic peak (0.38). That is not a mistake. The maximum of a noisy path selects its upward excursions, so the mean of the maxima exceeds the maximum of the mean. Anyone fitting a deterministic model to individually observed peaks will tend to overestimate production.

7 What it teaches and what it does not

Three equations are enough to organise the intuition: the reflex acts as a brake proportional to the threat, its absence amplifies and delays the response, and its main effect on variability is to compress the upper tail. But the model ignores almost everything else: anti-inflammatory cytokines, the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, tissue damage and the sympathetic branch. And efferent vagal activity is not directly observable in humans; indices derived from heart rate variability are, at best, noisy and indirect measurements of .

That last point defines the next problem: estimating the parameters of Equation 1 from partial, noisy observations is a problem of inference in state-space models, which is where the Bayesian methods and the stochastic processes of the previous posts meet.

Cite as Matías Castillo-Aguilar (2026). The inflammatory reflex as a stochastic dynamical system. Drift & Diffusion, 1(11).

Back to top

References

[1]
K. J. Tracey, “The inflammatory reflex,” Nature, vol. 420, no. 6917, pp. 853–859, 2002, doi: 10.1038/nature01321.
[2]
L. V. Borovikova et al., “Vagus nerve stimulation attenuates the systemic inflammatory response to endotoxin,” Nature, vol. 405, no. 6785, pp. 458–462, 2000, doi: 10.1038/35013070.
[3]
A. Reynolds, J. Rubin, G. Clermont, J. Day, Y. Vodovotz, and G. B. Ermentrout, “A reduced mathematical model of the acute inflammatory response: I. Derivation of model and analysis of anti-inflammation,” Journal of Theoretical Biology, vol. 242, no. 1, pp. 220–236, 2006, doi: 10.1016/j.jtbi.2006.02.016.

item.title: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process: noise with memory
item.dc:creator: Matías Castillo-Aguilar
item.description:
Original Article · Vol. I · No. 11 · November 2026

1 One equation, two forces

Almost no physiological variable stays still, and almost none wanders off without bound: it fluctuates around an equilibrium that something pulls it back to. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process [1] is the simplest mathematical form of that idea:

The first term is the drift: a restoring force that pushes towards with a strength proportional to the distance. The second is the diffusion: the increments of a Brownian motion , which perturb it relentlessly. The parameter has units of frequency, and its inverse is the time constant with which the system forgets a perturbation.

2 Exact solution

Unlike most stochastic differential equations, Equation 1 can be solved in closed form [2].

Proposition 1 (Transition distribution) For and initial condition ,

Proof. Let . By Itô’s formula, : the drift cancels. Integrating and rearranging,

The stochastic integral of a deterministic integrand is Gaussian with mean zero and, by the Itô isometry, its variance is .

Two immediate consequences. As the process forgets where it started and reaches the stationary distribution . And in that regime the autocovariance decays exponentially,

which is exactly what “noise with memory” means.

3 Simulation

Equation 2 gives an exact simulation scheme for any step : just sample the Gaussian transition. The generic alternative, valid for any equation, is the Euler–Maruyama scheme [3], which replaces differentials by finite increments.

ou_exact <- function(n, dt, theta, mu, sigma, x0) {
  a <- exp(-theta * dt)
  s <- sigma * sqrt((1 - a^2) / (2 * theta))
  x <- numeric(n + 1)
  x[1] <- x0
  z <- rnorm(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x[i + 1] <- mu + (x[i] - mu) * a + s * z[i]
  x
}

ou_euler <- function(n, dt, theta, mu, sigma, x0) {
  x <- numeric(n + 1)
  x[1] <- x0
  z <- rnorm(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    x[i + 1] <- x[i] + theta * (mu - x[i]) * dt + sigma * sqrt(dt) * z[i]
  }
  x
}

Fig. 1 shows twelve paths starting far from equilibrium, together with the mean and the standard deviation band predicted by Equation 2.

set.seed(1930)
theta <- 1; mu <- 0; sigma <- 1; x0 <- 4
dt <- 0.02
tt <- seq(0, 8, by = dt)

paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:12, function(k) {
  data.frame(t = tt, k = k,
             x = ou_exact(length(tt) - 1, dt, theta, mu, sigma, x0))
}))
theory <- data.frame(
  t = tt,
  m = mu + (x0 - mu) * exp(-theta * tt),
  s = sqrt(sigma^2 / (2 * theta) * (1 - exp(-2 * theta * tt)))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(t, ymin = m - 2 * s, ymax = m + 2 * s), theory,
              fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.22) +
  geom_line(aes(t, x, group = k), paths, linewidth = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(aes(t, x), subset(paths, k == 1), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(t, m), theory, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = expression("Time (in units of " * 1 / theta * ")"),
       y = expression(X[t]))

4 The Euler–Maruyama bias

Does it matter which scheme we use? Euler–Maruyama applied to Equation 1 is an autoregressive process with coefficient and innovation variance , whose stationary variance is

The scheme inflates the variance by a factor , and becomes unstable when . We check this by simulating long series with both schemes.

steps <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5)
n <- 2e5

bias <- do.call(rbind, lapply(steps, function(h) {
  data.frame(
    h = h,
    scheme = c("Euler–Maruyama", "Exact"),
    ratio = c(var(ou_euler(n, h, 1, 0, 1, 0)),
              var(ou_exact(n, h, 1, 0, 1, 0))) / 0.5   # exact: 1 / (2 · 1)
  )
}))

ggplot(bias, aes(h, ratio)) +
  geom_function(fun = function(h) 2 / (2 - h), colour = "grey45") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = scheme), size = 2.2, fill = "white") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Euler–Maruyama" = 16, "Exact" = 21)) +
  labs(x = expression(theta * Delta),
       y = "Simulated variance / exact variance")

With the excess is already 5%. The rule of thumb: if the equation is linear, always use the exact transition; if it is not, choose at least an order of magnitude below the fastest time constant in the system.

5 Estimating the parameters

Observed at regular intervals , an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process is exactly an AR(1):

Conditional maximum likelihood therefore reduces to a linear regression of each observation on the previous one, followed by inverting Equation 5.

fit_ou <- function(x, dt) {
  x0 <- x[-length(x)]
  x1 <- x[-1]
  b <- cov(x0, x1) / var(x0)
  a <- mean(x1) - b * mean(x0)
  s2 <- mean((x1 - a - b * x0)^2)
  theta <- -log(b) / dt
  c(theta = theta, mu = a / (1 - b), sigma = sqrt(2 * theta * s2 / (1 - b^2)))
}

As a toy example, think of an RR interval fluctuating around 850 ms with a time constant of 5 s, recorded once per second for ten minutes.

set.seed(1930)
truth <- c(theta = 0.2, mu = 850, sigma = 20)
x <- ou_exact(600, 1, truth[["theta"]], truth[["mu"]], truth[["sigma"]], 850)

estimate <- fit_ou(x, dt = 1)
tab <- rbind(Truth = truth, Estimate = estimate)
colnames(tab) <- c("$\\theta$ (1/s)", "$\\mu$ (ms)",
                   "$\\sigma$ (ms/$\\sqrt{\\text{s}}$)")
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3)

6 The hard parameter

The previous example had a series of 120 time constants on its side. With short recordings the story changes, because information about does not depend on the number of observations but on how many times the process managed to return to its mean. We check this by repeating the fit over thousands of series of two durations, with the same step .

set.seed(1930)
estimate_theta <- function(n, dt = 0.1) {
  x <- ou_exact(n, dt, 1, 0, 1, rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(0.5)))
  fit_ou(x, dt)[["theta"]]
}

mc <- rbind(
  data.frame(series = "short", theta = replicate(3000, estimate_theta(100))),
  data.frame(series = "long", theta = replicate(3000, estimate_theta(1000)))
)

ggplot(mc, aes(theta, linetype = series)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.55, bw = "SJ", key_glyph = "path") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(short = "dashed", long = "solid"),
    breaks = c("short", "long"),
    labels = expression(T == 10 / theta, T == 100 / theta)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(theta) / theta), y = "Density")

With ten time constants, the estimator overestimates by 47% on average and its standard deviation is 0.67: the data barely pin down its order of magnitude. With a hundred, the bias falls to 4% and the spread to 0.16. Sampling faster does not help; recording for longer does.

7 A physiological reading

The stationary variance mixes two different things: how much noise comes in () and how strongly it is corrected (). A system with and has exactly the same standard deviation (31.6) as another with and , but the second forgets ten times faster. An index of total variability cannot tell them apart; the autocorrelation in Equation 3 can. Separating how much it fluctuates from how fast it is regulated is precisely what a dynamical model adds to a descriptive statistic.

In the next post we use this process as one piece of a larger model: an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck vagal tone whose mean is no longer constant, because the immune system moves it.

Cite as Matías Castillo-Aguilar (2026). The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process: noise with memory. Drift & Diffusion, 1(11).

Back to top

References

[1]
G. E. Uhlenbeck and L. S. Ornstein, “On the theory of the Brownian motion,” Physical Review, vol. 36, no. 5, pp. 823–841, 1930, doi: 10.1103/PhysRev.36.823.
[2]
S. Särkkä and A. Solin, Applied stochastic differential equations. Cambridge University Press, 2019. doi: 10.1017/9781108186735.
[3]
P. E. Kloeden and E. Platen, Numerical solution of stochastic differential equations. Berlin: Springer, 1992. doi: 10.1007/978-3-662-12616-5.

item.title: How fast does the heart recover? Metropolis–Hastings from scratch
item.dc:creator: Matías Castillo-Aguilar
item.description:
Original Article · Vol. I · No. 10 · October 2026

1 The problem

When exercise stops, heart rate does not drop at once: it descends towards rest along a roughly exponential curve. The early part of that descent mostly reflects vagal reactivation [1], and a slow recovery over the first minute is associated with higher mortality [2]. The speed of recovery is therefore a cheap, non-invasive window onto the autonomic control of the heart.

The simplest model that captures the idea is

where is the resting rate, the amplitude of the descent and the time constant: the number of seconds heart rate takes to cover 63% of the way back. We want to estimate and, above all, to know how much we know about it.

2 Data with a known truth

To be able to check the method we simulate a five-minute recovery, sampled every five seconds, with parameters we know.

set.seed(1930)

hr_mean <- function(t, hr_rest, A, tau) hr_rest + A * exp(-t / tau)

truth <- c(hr_rest = 68, A = 62, tau = 75, sigma = 3)
t <- seq(0, 300, by = 5)
y <- hr_mean(t, 68, 62, 75) + rnorm(length(t), 0, truth[["sigma"]])
dat <- data.frame(t, y)

ggplot(dat, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_function(fun = hr_mean, args = list(hr_rest = 68, A = 62, tau = 75),
                linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Time since end of exercise (s)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)")

3 The Bayesian model

Three of the four parameters are positive. Rather than imposing constraints, we work on an unconstrained scale,

and place the priors directly on :

These priors rule out the physiologically absurd and little else. By Bayes’ theorem, the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior,

and in R all we need is its logarithm:

log_posterior <- function(phi, t, y) {
  mu <- phi[1] + exp(phi[2]) * exp(-t / exp(phi[3]))
  sum(dnorm(y, mu, exp(phi[4]), log = TRUE)) +   # likelihood
    dnorm(phi[1], 70, 15, log = TRUE) +           # priors
    dnorm(phi[2], log(60), 0.5, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(phi[3], log(60), 0.75, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(phi[4], log(3), 1, log = TRUE)
}

4 Metropolis in twenty lines

The normalising constant of Equation 2 is a four-dimensional integral that we never need to compute. The Metropolis algorithm [3], [4] builds a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior using only ratios of densities, in which that constant cancels.

Definition 1 (Random-walk Metropolis) Given the current state :

  1. propose , with ;
  2. accept the proposal with probability ;
  3. if rejected, repeat as the next state.
metropolis <- function(log_post, init, n_iter, step, ...) {
  d <- length(init)
  chain <- matrix(NA_real_, n_iter, d)
  current <- init
  lp <- log_post(current, ...)
  accepted <- 0L
  for (i in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    proposal <- current + rnorm(d, 0, step)
    lp_prop <- log_post(proposal, ...)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp) {          # accept with probability α
      current <- proposal
      lp <- lp_prop
      accepted <- accepted + 1L
    }
    chain[i, ] <- current
  }
  list(chain = chain, acceptance = accepted / n_iter)
}

We launch four chains from dispersed starting points. The step sizes in step were tuned by hand until the acceptance rate fell within the range regarded as efficient: between 0.23, the theoretical optimum in high dimension [5], and 0.44, the optimum for a single parameter.

n_iter <- 30000
step <- c(0.45, 0.02, 0.04, 0.09)

chains <- lapply(1:4, function(k) {
  init <- c(rnorm(1, 70, 10), log(60) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.4),
            log(60) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.6), log(3) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5))
  metropolis(log_posterior, init, n_iter, step, t = t, y = y)
})

round(sapply(chains, `[[`, "acceptance"), 3)
#> [1] 0.281 0.283 0.284 0.286

5 Did it converge?

Before looking at results, the chains deserve some distrust. Fig. 2 shows the first iterations of : all four forget their starting point within a few hundred steps and then mix together.

traces <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(k) {
  data.frame(iter = 1:3000, tau = exp(chains[[k]]$chain[1:3000, 3]),
             chain = factor(k))
}))

ggplot(traces, aes(iter, tau, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dd_tinta, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = expression(tau ~ "(s, log scale)"))

We discard the first half of each chain as warm-up and compute the statistic [6], which compares between-chain and within-chain variance; values close to 1 indicate that all chains describe the same distribution.

posterior <- lapply(chains, function(x) x$chain[(n_iter / 2 + 1):n_iter, ])

rhat <- function(lst, j) {
  m <- sapply(lst, function(x) x[, j])
  n <- nrow(m)
  B <- n * var(colMeans(m))            # between-chain variance
  W <- mean(apply(m, 2, var))          # within-chain variance
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}

setNames(round(sapply(1:4, rhat, lst = posterior), 3),
         c("hr_rest", "log_A", "log_tau", "log_sigma"))
#>   hr_rest     log_A   log_tau log_sigma 
#>     1.005     1.000     1.005     1.000

6 What we learned

We pool the four chains and return to the natural scale.

phi <- do.call(rbind, posterior)
draws <- data.frame(hr_rest = phi[, 1], A = exp(phi[, 2]),
                    tau = exp(phi[, 3]), sigma = exp(phi[, 4]))

tab <- t(sapply(draws, resumen_posterior))
tab <- cbind(truth = truth[rownames(tab)], tab)
rownames(tab) <- c("$\\mathrm{HR}_\\infty$ (bpm)", "$A$ (bpm)",
                   "$\\tau$ (s)", "$\\sigma$ (bpm)")

knitr::kable(tab, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Truth", "Mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%"))

The posterior mean of is 74.0 s, with a 95% credible interval from 66.7 to 82.0 s, which contains the true value of 75 s. Fig. 3 shows the whole Bayesian update: a prior that allowed anything from 14 to 261 s ends up, after 61 observations, concentrated in a range of about 15 seconds.

grid <- data.frame(tau = seq(20, 160, length.out = 400))
grid$prior <- dlnorm(grid$tau, log(60), 0.75)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(tau, prior, linetype = "Prior"), grid, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_density(aes(tau, linetype = "Posterior"), draws, fill = "grey60",
               alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.55, key_glyph = "path") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 75, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 160)) +
  labs(x = expression(tau ~ "(s)"), y = "Density")

A more demanding check is the posterior predictive: simulate new data from the fitted model and see whether they look like the observed ones.

sub <- draws[sample(nrow(draws), 2000), ]
tg <- seq(0, 300, by = 2)

curves <- sapply(tg, function(s) hr_mean(s, sub$hr_rest, sub$A, sub$tau))
new_y <- curves + rnorm(length(curves), 0, sub$sigma)

band <- function(m) apply(m, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
pred <- data.frame(t = tg, mean = colMeans(curves),
                   c_lo = band(curves)[1, ], c_hi = band(curves)[2, ],
                   y_lo = band(new_y)[1, ], y_hi = band(new_y)[2, ])

ggplot(pred, aes(t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = y_lo, ymax = y_hi), fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = c_lo, ymax = c_hi), fill = "grey20", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean)) +
  geom_point(aes(t, y), dat, size = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Time since end of exercise (s)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)")

7 From parameters to the clinical index

The practical advantage of having posterior draws is that the uncertainty of any derived quantity comes for free. The usual clinical index is heart rate recovery at one minute,

and its posterior distribution is obtained by applying Equation 3 to every draw:

hrr60 <- draws$A * (1 - exp(-60 / draws$tau))
round(resumen_posterior(hrr60), 1)
#> media    de   inf   sup 
#>  33.3   1.4  30.6  36.2

That is, 33.3 bpm, with a 95% interval from 30.6 to 36.2 bpm (the true value is 34.1). No delta method or asymptotic approximation was needed.

8 Limits and what comes next

Two honest caveats. The first is statistical: and are strongly correlated in the posterior ( -0.83), because a slower recovery towards a lower resting rate looks very much like a faster one towards a higher resting rate. A random walk with independent steps explores such diagonal ridges poorly; that is why a four-parameter problem needed tens of thousands of iterations. Hamiltonian methods handle this far better.

The second is physiological: Equation 1 assumes independent errors, but real heart rate fluctuates with memory. Neighbouring beats resemble each other. Ignoring this makes the intervals too optimistic. The remedy is to model the noise as a stochastic process with temporal correlation, and the simplest of them all is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.
